tldr: This paper resolves the jerky motion problem Diffusion Policy suffers from during plan transitions by predicting cumulative B-spline control poses on SE(3) and sharing boundary control poses via inpainting. This guarantees $C^2$ continuity across the entire planned trajectory. In real-robot experiments, it reduced jerk by more than an order of magnitude and dramatically improved success rates on tasks involving liquids and flexible objects.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of LieSpline-DP. Control pose coordinates are predicted by a diffusion model in a local tangent space anchored at the observed pose, while an inpainting process fixes a boundary prefix inherited from the previous execution. The resulting control poses are lifted to $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ and reconstructed into a smooth end-effector trajectory via cumulative B-splines.
overview:
Diffusion Policy (DP) is a prominent imitation learning framework capable of capturing complex multimodal actions with high precision. However, when deployed asynchronously on real robots—regenerating and replanning action chunks on the fly to hide latency—the trajectory becomes discontinuous at chunk boundaries, causing severe jerk and vibrations.

To address this, the authors propose LieSpline-DP, which represents trajectories as continuous B-spline curves directly on the special Euclidean group $\mathrm{SE}(3)$, rather than discrete sequences of waypoints. While B-splines are mathematically smooth, simply stitching independently predicted chunks does not guarantee boundary smoothness. LieSpline-DP fixes the boundary control poses from the previous plan and generates only the remaining future control points via inpainting. By aligning a shared knot vector, it mathematically guarantees $C^2$ continuity (continuity up to acceleration) across consecutive plans without any post-processing, blending, or refitting.

In evaluations across simulation (Robomimic) and a real UR5e robot, LieSpline-DP reduced trajectory jerk by over 80% in simulation. In three real-robot tasks—beaker pouring, bucket hooking with a suspended hook, and cube stacking—where the DP baseline frequently failed due to splashing water or swinging ropes, LieSpline-DP achieved a 100% success rate on both pouring and bucket hooking. The work clearly demonstrates how trajectory smoothness is critical for stabilizing real-world physical dynamics.
contributions: Proposed a framework that directly predicts cumulative B-spline control poses on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ via a diffusion model in local coordinates for robot end-effector motion.
Mathematically guaranteed $C^2$ continuity across asynchronous replanning without post-processing by reusing and fixing boundary control poses from previous plans as prefixes.
Developed a dataset conversion pipeline using event-weighted optimization and latency alignment to extract prefix-target pairs from dense demonstrations.
Demonstrated over an order-of-magnitude reduction in trajectory jerk on a real robot, dramatically outperforming the DP baseline on challenging tasks involving liquids and flexible objects.

sections.heading: Why does Diffusion Policy produce jerky motions?
sections.summary: To hide inference latency on real robots, Diffusion Policy asynchronously replans trajectory chunks. However, independently generated chunks cause boundary discontinuities and vibrations. Existing spline and ensembling methods fail to strictly guarantee cross-chunk $C^2$ continuity or respect the geometry of $\mathrm{SE}(3)$.
sections.details:
Diffusion Policy (DP) has achieved remarkable success in imitation learning. Typically, DP outputs fixed-horizon action chunks and predicts the next chunk while executing a portion of the current one. Because real robots suffer from inference latency, asynchronous execution—predicting the next chunk in parallel while executing current actions—is essential. However, switching between independently generated chunks introduces velocity and acceleration discontinuities. This leads to severe jerk, tracking errors, and task failures.

To mitigate this, methods like ACT use temporal ensembling to take a weighted average of overlapping predictions. Yet, averaging can blend distinct multimodal modes and cause blurriness. Other approaches, such as Stateful Diffusion (conditioning on past actions) or RTC (fixing executed prefixes), operate on discrete action sequences and cannot explicitly guarantee velocity or acceleration continuity.

Spline-based action representations have also been explored. However, prior methods (like BEAST or ABPolicy) either only maintain position continuity ($C^0$) or rely on approximate least-squares refitting, lacking theoretical guarantees for $C^2$ continuity (smooth up to acceleration). Furthermore, most existing methods treat poses as Euclidean vectors, ignoring the Lie group structure of $\mathrm{SE}(3)$. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces LieSpline-DP, which formulates B-splines directly on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ and achieves cross-chunk $C^2$ continuity by sharing boundary control poses.

sections.heading: Mathematical foundations: Diffusion models and B-splines on SE(3)
sections.summary: This section reviews conditional generation and inpainting with diffusion models. It also covers the exponential and logarithmic maps of $\mathrm{SE}(3)$, and defines cumulative Lie-group B-spline trajectories for rigid-body end-effector motion.
sections.details:
### II-A Diffusion Policy
Diffusion models capture conditional distributions through a forward process that gradually adds noise to clean action representations $\mathbf{x}^{(0)}$, and a reverse process that denoises them. During training, a denoising network $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}$ is optimized to predict the injected noise given noisy actions and observation context $\mathcal{O}$. At inference time, known action components can be overwritten and held fixed after each denoising step via inpainting, enabling coherent generation conditioned on a fixed prefix.

### II-B Geometry of SE(3) B-spline Trajectories
A robot end-effector pose is represented as an element $T$ of the special Euclidean group $\mathrm{SE}(3)$, consisting of rotation $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ and translation $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Incremental twists $\boldsymbol{\xi} = [\boldsymbol{\rho}^\top, \boldsymbol{\phi}^\top]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^6$ are mapped to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ via the exponential map $\operatorname{Exp}$ and logarithmic map $\operatorname{Log}$. This paper uses the right-multiplication convention $T \operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ for relative transformations.

Given a sequence of control poses $\mathcal{Q} = (Q_0, \dots, Q_{H-1})$, relative twists between adjacent poses are defined as $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j = \operatorname{Log}(Q_{j-1}^{-1} Q_j)$. The cumulative Lie-group B-spline trajectory $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}(s)$ on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ is constructed as a product of group elements exponentiated by cumulative basis functions $\beta_{j,p}(s)$ of degree $p$. Using uniform knot vectors with unit spacing $\tau_i = i$ ensures that local basis functions maintain compact and well-defined support.

sections.heading: LieSpline-DP: Inpainting SE(3) control poses with guaranteed C² continuity
sections.summary: Control poses are represented in a local tangent space centered at the observed pose. Future points are inpainted while fixing poses inherited from the prior plan. Combining a shared knot vector with the reuse of three boundary control poses turns the entire asynchronous plan into a single, smooth $C^2$ spline.
sections.details:
### III-A Overview
The overall framework of LieSpline-DP is illustrated in Fig. F2. In planning cycle $n$, the end-effector trajectory is parameterized by $H = K + F$ control poses $\mathcal{Q}_n$ on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ ($K = p = 3$ for cubic splines, with $F$ future predictions). Using the robot's current observed pose $T_n^{\mathrm{obs}}$ as the anchor $Q_n^{\mathrm{anchor}}$, the diffusion model operates over 6D local coordinates $\mathcal{Z}_n = (\mathbf{z}_{n,0}, \dots, \mathbf{z}_{n,H-1})$ in its local tangent space. The first $K$ poses serve as a fixed prefix inherited from the previous plan, while the remaining $F$ future control points are generated using block-causal self-attention and cross-attention over observations.

### III-B Asynchronous Inference Pipeline
The local coordinate system is defined as $\mathbf{z}_{n,j} = \operatorname{Log}((Q_n^{\mathrm{anchor}})^{-1} Q_{n,j})$. Anchoring at an observed pose close to the target trajectory maintains accurate local linearization, stabilizing Gaussian noise injection and denoising. Changing anchors between plans merely re-expresses absolute poses without affecting the physical trajectory boundary.

Smoothness is guaranteed through a shared knot grid and boundary control pose reuse. Cubic B-splines ($p=3$) are inherently $C^2$-continuous (continuous in position, velocity, and acceleration) across knot spans. When transitioning from plan $n$ to plan $n+1$ at a handover point shifted by $E$ control steps, the last $K=p=3$ control poses of plan $n$ are reused as the prefix of plan $n+1$. This connects consecutive plans using identical local basis functions, strictly preserving $C^2$ continuity across the entire trajectory without any post-hoc blending or refitting.

### III-C Spline Dataset Conversion and Training
To prevent dataset shrinkage caused by downsampling dense demonstrations every $S$ steps, sub-episodes are generated by shifting the starting offset $\delta \in \{0, \dots, S-1\}$. For each sub-episode, an optimization problem with event weights $w$ (e.g., gripper open/close events) is solved to fit an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ spline that balances tracking accuracy at key events with overall smoothness. Finally, windows are extracted considering real-robot inference latency $L$, producing a training dataset perfectly aligned with the timing of asynchronous execution.

captions.F2: Model architecture and spline reconstruction flow in LieSpline-DP. On the left, KV caches are computed from image observations and robot poses. In the center, a Transformer denoiser inpaints future control points (light purple) conditioned on a fixed prefix (dark purple). On the right, these control points are lifted back to $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ and evaluated as a continuous cumulative B-spline trajectory.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-robot evaluations: Remarkable smoothness and task success
sections.summary: After validating an over 80% reduction in trajectory jerk on the Robomimic benchmark, LieSpline-DP was tested on a real UR5e arm across three tasks: pouring, bucket hooking, and cube stacking. It dramatically improved success rates over the DP baseline, especially in tasks involving liquids and flexible objects.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation
LieSpline-DP was evaluated against a dense-waypoint DP baseline across four Robomimic tasks (Lift, Can, Square, and Tool Hang). With matched network architectures and training setups, LieSpline-DP reduced 95th-percentile (p95) end-effector jerk by more than 80% in translation and 85% in rotation. Task success rates were comparable on coarser manipulation tasks like Lift and Can, but slightly lower on Square and Tool Hang, which require millimeter-level precise alignment.

### IV-B Real Robot
Experiments were conducted on a real UR5e robot with a Unitree Dex1 gripper running at 15 Hz across three real-world tasks (Fig. F4), with 20 trials each:
- **Pouring**: Grasping a water-filled beaker and pouring into a target beaker without spilling. LieSpline-DP achieved 20/20 (100%) success, compared to only 2/20 (10%) for the DP baseline. Jerky motions from DP caused significant water sloshing, pushing visual observations out of the demonstration distribution and causing the robot to freeze mid-trajectory.
- **Bucket hooking**: Maneuvering a flexible suspended hook to catch a bucket handle and transport it. LieSpline-DP achieved 20/20 (100%) success, while DP reached only 6/20 (30%). Sudden movements from DP induced violent rope swings that the policy could not recover from.
- **Cube stacking**: Stacking three cubes in a specified color order at a target location. LieSpline-DP achieved 16/20 (80%) success versus 11/20 (55%) for DP, avoiding micro-vibrations that knocked over stacked cubes. In additional disturbance tests where cubes were manually disrupted, LieSpline-DP autonomously recovered and completed the task in 7 out of 10 trials.

Across all real-world tasks, LieSpline-DP's commanded p95 jerk was more than an order of magnitude lower than DP's, confirming its exceptional trajectory smoothness.

### IV-C Discussion
While DP was competitive in precise simulation benchmarks, LieSpline-DP outperformed DP across all three real-robot tasks. Physical dynamics overlooked in simulation—such as liquid sloshing and flexible object oscillations triggered by jerky motions—become catastrophic failure points in the real world. These findings strongly demonstrate that intrinsic trajectory smoothness is vital for real-world robustness.

captions.F4: Sequential snapshots of the three real-robot evaluation tasks. (a) Pouring water from a beaker, (b) hooking and transporting a bucket using a rope-suspended hook, and (c) sequentially stacking three colored cubes. Smooth trajectory control is critical for success in all three tasks.

sections.heading: Limitations and future directions: Extending to other backbones and test-time optimization
sections.summary: While implemented with a Transformer-based diffusion policy, this approach can extend to Flow Matching or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. Integrating compact control pose representations with test-time trajectory optimization (obstacle avoidance and constraint satisfaction) is another promising avenue.
sections.details:
Although the $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ spline formulation is agnostic to the underlying generative architecture, this work evaluated it solely within a Transformer-based Diffusion Policy. Future work includes integrating this approach into Flow Matching policies or large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to test generalization across diverse architectures and tasks.

Additionally, representing trajectories with a compact set of control poses instead of dense waypoints is well-suited for test-time planning as inference. Because of the local support property of B-splines, modifying individual control points preserves overall trajectory smoothness without destabilizing the plan. This opens exciting possibilities for compactly optimizing constraints, such as obstacle avoidance and joint limits, directly during inference.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.summary: LieSpline-DP adopts cumulative cubic B-splines on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ as action representations and guarantees cross-chunk $C^2$ continuity by sharing boundary control poses. It reduces jerk by an order of magnitude on a real robot and demonstrates superior success rates on complex manipulation tasks involving liquids and flexible objects.
sections.details: This paper presented LieSpline-DP, modeling robot end-effector trajectories directly as cumulative cubic B-splines on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$. By inheriting and fixing boundary control poses from previous plans and inpainting future control points during asynchronous replanning, the method mathematically guarantees $C^2$ continuity across the entire trajectory without post-processing. Real-robot experiments demonstrated drastic reductions in trajectory jerk and decisive advantages over the DP baseline in real-world tasks where smoothness is essential, such as pouring (100% vs. 10%) and bucket hooking (100% vs. 30%).

takeaways: Asynchronous replanning policies can mathematically guarantee $C^2$ continuity (acceleration continuity) across chunk boundaries simply by inheriting three B-spline control poses, without any post-processing.
Even when overlooked in simulation benchmarks, trajectory jerk in the real world causes catastrophic failures when manipulating dynamic objects like liquids and ropes.
Running diffusion models in a local tangent space anchored at the observed pose preserves $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ geometry and enables remarkably stable end-effector trajectory generation.
limitations: Due to the compact spline representation, expressive capacity may be slightly constrained compared to dense waypoint predictions in tasks requiring millimeter-level, sharp adjustments (e.g., Robomimic's Square and Tool Hang).
Evaluations in this paper are limited to Transformer-based diffusion models; extending and validating the method with other modern policy architectures like Flow Matching or VLAs remains future work.
The dataset preparation pipeline requires careful tuning and multi-step processing, including control pose fitting and latency alignment.
